**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Time allowed: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section. All questions carry twenty-five marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples. Only the required number of questions will be marked. Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Structure of the paper: SECTION A: Physical Geography (questions 1 to 3); SECTION B: Human Geography (questions 4 to 6); SECTION C: Contemporary Environmental and Development Issues (question 7, with an EITHER/OR choice between two sets of sub-questions).

questions.enonce_markdown:
**EITHER**

(a) Explain briefly the meaning of El Nino.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Meaning.** **El Niño** is the periodic warming of the surface water of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, which occurs every few years (roughly every 2 to 7 years) and usually lasts about a year. It forms part of the **El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO)** cycle, in which changes in ocean temperature are linked with changes in atmospheric pressure and winds across the Pacific. The name ("the Christ child") was given by Peruvian fishermen who noticed the warm water arriving off the coast around Christmas.

![fig-1](gce-al-geography-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_7_fig_1.png)

**Normal conditions.** The strong easterly trade winds push warm surface water west towards Indonesia and northern Australia, building up a warm pool there with heavy rain and rising air. Off the coast of Peru, the surface water that is blown away is replaced by cold, nutrient-rich water from below (**upwelling**, the Humboldt/Peru current), which supports a rich fishery and keeps the coast dry.

**During El Niño.** The trade winds weaken (or reverse), the warm water spreads back eastwards across the Pacific, and the thermocline deepens in the east. Upwelling is reduced or stopped, the sea off Peru and Ecuador warms by several degrees, fish catches collapse, and heavy rain falls over the usually arid coast of Peru and Ecuador, while Indonesia and Australia experience drought. These changes alter weather patterns around the world (floods in some regions, droughts in others).

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) State **two** areas in the world where El Nino occurs.
questions.corrige_markdown:
El Niño originates in the tropical Pacific Ocean, and its effects extend to many regions through changes in the atmosphere (teleconnections).

**Two areas where El Niño occurs:**
1. **The eastern equatorial Pacific off the coasts of Peru and Ecuador (western South America)**, where the warm surface water replaces the cold upwelling water and heavy rain and floods follow.
2. **The central equatorial Pacific Ocean (towards the International Date Line)**, the region of the warming in the central Pacific (the area monitored for the sea-surface temperature anomaly), from which the warm water spreads east.

**Areas strongly affected (teleconnections).** Indonesia, the Philippines and northern and eastern Australia (drought and bush fires); India and South-East Asia (weak monsoon in some years); south-eastern Africa and southern Africa (drought); parts of East Africa (heavy rain and floods); the southern United States (wetter than normal) and parts of northern South America (drought).

**Introduction.** Deforestation is the permanent clearing of forest, mainly for farming (shifting cultivation, cocoa and oil palm plantations), logging, firewood and charcoal, mining and the building of roads and settlements. It is serious in the Congo Basin forests (in Cameroon, mainly in the South and East) and in the savanna woodland of the north where firewood is cut. Two consequences:

**1. Soil erosion, floods and siltation of rivers.**
- Without the canopy and the roots, heavy rain hits the bare soil directly (splash erosion), runoff increases, and the thin fertile topsoil is washed away (sheet and gully erosion, landslides on slopes), so fertility is lost and farming yields fall.
- Less interception and infiltration mean that water reaches rivers quickly, so floods become more frequent and severe, while dry-season flow can decrease. The eroded soil silts up rivers, lakes, dams and harbours, harms fish and increases flood risk downstream.

**2. Loss of biodiversity and climatic effects.**
- Forests are the habitat of a great number of plant and animal species (the Cameroon rainforest has forest elephants, gorillas and chimpanzees and countless plants). Clearing destroys habitats and food sources, so species are lost (some before they are even known) and the genetic resources and medicines they contain are lost. Local people also lose forest products (food, fuel, medicines).
- Trees store carbon and release water vapour by transpiration. Cutting and burning them release carbon dioxide (adding to the greenhouse effect and global warming), and the loss of transpiration reduces local rainfall, so the local climate becomes hotter and drier. In extreme cases, cleared land can become degraded or desert-like.

**Other consequences (if needed):** lowering of the water table, loss of income and of livelihoods, and conflicts over land.

**Conclusion.** Deforestation has local effects (erosion, floods, loss of fertility) and global effects (loss of biodiversity, climate change).

questions.enonce_markdown: ii) What measures would you recommend to reduce the effects of deforestation?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Recommended measures** (any well explained set, in the order of importance):

1. **Reafforestation and afforestation.** Replant cleared and degraded land with native and fast-growing species, protect natural regeneration, and plant woodlots and shelter belts. This restores soil, water and wildlife, and absorbs carbon.
2. **Sustainable forest management and laws.** Control logging through quotas, selective felling, replanting obligations, management plans and certification of timber, and enforce the laws against illegal logging with inspections and penalties. Cameroon's 1994 forestry law introduced management plans, forest royalties and **community forests**, so that local people have an interest in conserving the forest.
3. **Protected areas.** Create and effectively protect national parks and reserves (such as the Korup National Park and the Dja Faunal Reserve), with the support of local communities.
4. **Reducing the demand for wood and forest land.** Introduce improved cooking stoves, gas and solar energy to reduce firewood and charcoal use; use **agroforestry**, crop rotation and improved seeds and fertiliser to raise yields on existing farmland, so less forest is cleared; use wood waste efficiently.
5. **Education, participation and international support.** Educate the population on the value of forests, involve them in forest management, and use international aid and schemes that pay for forest conservation (for example carbon-credit and REDD+ projects).

**Conclusion.** The best approach combines protection and replanting with laws that are enforced and with alternatives that reduce pressure on the forest and give local people a benefit.

**Definition.** A **trade bloc** is a group of countries, usually in the same region, that agree to reduce or remove barriers to trade among themselves (tariffs, quotas, administrative restrictions) in order to increase trade and economic growth, and which often apply a common policy towards countries outside the group. It is a form of **regional economic integration**.

**Levels of integration (from the loosest to the closest).**
1. **Preferential trade area**: members give each other lower tariffs on some goods.
2. **Free trade area**: tariffs and quotas between members are removed, but each member keeps its own tariffs against non-members (for example the USMCA of the United States, Mexico and Canada, and the African Continental Free Trade Area, AfCFTA).
3. **Customs union**: a free trade area with a **common external tariff** for imports from outside (for example the CEMAC and the East African Community customs unions).
4. **Common (single) market**: also free movement of labour, capital and services (the European Union single market).
5. **Economic and monetary union**: a common currency and common economic policies (the Eurozone; the CEMAC and WAEMU use the CFA franc).
6. **Political union**: common government institutions (the European Union has some such features).

**Examples.** European Union (EU), ASEAN (South-East Asia), USMCA (North America), MERCOSUR (South America), ECOWAS (West Africa), CEMAC (Central Africa), SADC (southern Africa) and the East African Community.

**Reasons for forming them.** Larger markets and economies of scale, more trade and investment, greater bargaining power in world trade, political co-operation and peace, and cheaper goods for consumers.

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) With reference to any trade bloc, examine its objectives and problems encountered in its functioning.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Chosen bloc: CEMAC (Economic and Monetary Community of Central Africa).**

**Introduction.** The CEMAC was created by a treaty signed in 1994 and took effect in 1999, replacing the earlier Customs and Economic Union of Central Africa (UDEAC, created in the 1960s). It has six members: Cameroon, the Central African Republic, Chad, the Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea and Gabon. Its headquarters are in Bangui. Its member states share a currency, the Central African CFA franc, issued by the regional central bank (the BEAC, based in Yaoundé).

**Objectives**
1. **Free movement of goods, services, capital and persons** within the community, by abolishing customs duties and non-tariff barriers on products originating in the area, and by creating a **common external tariff** (customs union).
2. **Monetary union**: a common currency, a common central bank and a common monetary policy, to give stable prices and confidence in the currency.
3. **Economic integration and co-ordination** of national policies (agriculture, transport, industry, energy, trade and competition) and of regional programmes such as road and rail links.
4. **Promote the development and cooperation** of the sub-region: to enlarge the market of the member states (a market of tens of millions of consumers), to raise living standards, reduce poverty, and to strengthen the bargaining position of members in negotiations with others.
5. **Peace, solidarity and stability** among member states through economic partnership.

**Problems**
1. **Low intra-regional trade and similar economies.** Members produce similar primary products (oil, timber, cocoa, coffee, cotton), which they export to outside markets rather than to each other, so trade among them is very small; the economies are not complementary and manufacturing is weak. Most members depend on oil and commodity exports, so prices on the world market produce crises across the region (for example the fall in oil prices after 2014).
2. **Poor infrastructure and non-tariff barriers.** Roads and railways between member states are limited, in poor condition and landlocked members (Chad, Central African Republic) depend on routes through Cameroon (Douala port). There are numerous administrative checkpoints, delays, informal payments and customs formalities that increase costs despite the removal of duties. Free movement of persons is only partly implemented.
3. **Political instability and weak implementation.** Conflicts and instability (in the Central African Republic and Chad), weak institutions, late payment of members' contributions, a lack of political will and the failure to apply community decisions (members sometimes protect national interests) hinder integration. Overlapping memberships (ECCAS) cause confusion and duplication.
4. **External pressures and loss of national revenue.** Members lose customs revenue when tariffs are removed, and negotiations with large partners (the European Union's trade agreements) can create differences between members. The fixed link of the CFA franc to the euro is criticised as limiting competitiveness and monetary independence.

**Conclusion.** The CEMAC has important aims (a customs and monetary union, free movement and common policies), and the monetary union is functioning, but integration in trade and in the movement of people is limited by similar economies, poor infrastructure, non-tariff barriers, political instability and weak enforcement. A more diverse economy, better transport links and stronger political commitment would be needed to realise its objectives.

*(The same questions could be answered with the EU, whose single market and Eurozone are far more advanced but face problems of differences in wealth between members, sovereignty concerns and crises such as Brexit.)*
